fields.definition: The aggressive, buzzing, brassy timbre of a pipe organ's reed stops — ranks whose pipes sound by a vibrating brass tongue beating against a shallot rather than by an air jet — in which prominent upper harmonics give a raspy, snarling edge, most notably in chorus reeds such as the Trumpet, Bombarde or Trompeta.
fields.plain_english: On a pipe organ, some pipes make sound with a small vibrating metal tongue instead of a plain jet of air. These reed pipes have a buzzy, brassy growl. That harsh edge is called the snarl.
fields.purpose_function: Reed stops add power, bite and a brass-like voice to the organ chorus; the snarling edge lets them cut through full organ and carry solo lines over the smoother flue ranks.
fields.practical_application: An organist hears reed snarl when drawing chorus reeds for a big tutti, and a voicer or tuner sets the tongue curvature and tuning wire to keep the snarl even across the rank without turning harsh or spitting.
common_mistakes: Assuming every organ pipe is a reed; most stops are flue (labial) pipes that sound with an air jet, not a beating tongue.
Mistaking a musical reed snarl for a fault, when a rough, spitting or uneven reed usually means the tongue, tuning wire or shallot needs regulating.
Thinking the snarl comes from the resonator alone; the tongue and shallot set the buzz, and the resonator shapes and reinforces it.
scenario_contexts: Drawing chorus reeds like the Trumpet and Bombarde for a full-organ climax and hearing them snarl above the flue chorus.
A voicer regulating a new reed rank so the snarl is even from bass to treble.
A tuner curving the tongue and setting the tuning wire on a Trompeta to control brightness and edge.

sources: Audsley, The Art of Organ Building
Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (organ stop; reed pipes)
Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments (organ reed pipes)

fields.definition: The loud, piercing, buzzy tone of the rhaita (Maghrebi ghaita) and mizmar — conical-bore double-reed shawms of North Africa and the Arab world, related to the zurna — whose wide, open reed and flaring bell produce a penetrating, blaring sound suited to outdoor and ceremonial playing.
fields.plain_english: The rhaita and mizmar are loud folk oboes from North Africa and the Middle East. Their big double reed and open bell give a bright, buzzy blast that carries far outdoors. That piercing sound is the blare.
fields.purpose_function: The blaring tone lets these shawms lead outdoor processions, weddings and dances without amplification; the double reed and conical bore make the instrument naturally loud and rich in high harmonics.
fields.practical_application: An engineer capturing a rhaita or mizmar expects very high levels and sharp upper harmonics, so they pad the input, back the mic off and watch for harshness in the upper mids.
common_mistakes: Calling the rhaita or mizmar a single-reed instrument; both are double-reed shawms like the zurna, not clarinet-type instruments.
UNSAFE: Close-miking a rhaita or mizmar at full blare with no pad and no hearing protection; these shawms reach very high sound-pressure levels that risk hearing damage and input overload.
Treating the buzzy blare as distortion to be equalized away, when the strong high harmonics are the instrument's real voice.
scenario_contexts: Miking a mizmar in an Egyptian wedding band and adding a pad to handle the loud, piercing level.
A world-music session where the rhaita must sit over drums without swamping the mix.
An engineer gently taming harsh upper-mid blare while keeping the instrument's character.

sources: Baines, Woodwind Instruments and Their History
Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (ghaita; mizmar; zurna)
OSHA 29 CFR 1910.95 (occupational noise exposure)

fields.definition: Two expressive brass approaches to a note: a rip is a fast, aggressive upward flourish that races through the harmonic series into a target pitch, while a smear is a slower slide or bend that glides into or between pitches using lip and partial-valve control.
fields.plain_english: On brass instruments, a rip is a quick, rough slide up into a note. A smear is a slower slide or bend into it. Think of a trumpet player scooping up to a big note in a jazz band.
fields.purpose_function: Rips and smears add jazz and blues expression, letting brass players attack notes with excitement or ease instead of hitting them cleanly; they shape phrasing and style in big-band and pop writing.
fields.practical_application: An arranger notates a rip or smear so brass players know to slide into the note, and an engineer mixing the section leaves headroom for the loud, bright peak a rip lands on.
common_mistakes: Confusing a rip with a clean glissando; a rip is a fast, rough flourish through the harmonics, not a smooth continuous slide.
Playing a smear as a hard, in-tune interval, when the effect depends on bending lazily into the pitch rather than snapping to it.
Notating a rip with no target note, leaving the player unsure where the flourish should land.
scenario_contexts: A big-band trumpet section ripping up to a shout-chorus hit.
A trombonist smearing into a bluesy melody note.
An arranger marking rips and smears in a horn chart for a pop record.

sources: Adler, The Study of Orchestration
Kennan & Grantham, The Technique of Orchestration
Sebesky, The Contemporary Arranger

fields.definition: The rough, buzzing, gravelly bass tone of the serpent — a curved, leather-covered wooden lip-reed instrument of the cornett family with open finger holes — and of the ophicleide, its 19th-century keyed-brass successor; both are blown with a cup mouthpiece and noted for a coarse, rasping voice that filled the bass before the tuba.
fields.plain_english: The serpent and ophicleide are old bass horns you buzz your lips into, like a tuba's ancestors. Their sound is rough and buzzy. That gritty growl is called the rasp.
fields.purpose_function: These instruments supplied the bass voice in early wind bands, churches and orchestras before the tuba; the rasp comes from wide finger or key holes and a large cup mouthpiece that make the low notes speak with a coarse edge.
fields.practical_application: A player or engineer working with period instruments expects the serpent's and ophicleide's uneven, rasping low notes and mics them close to capture body without exaggerating the buzz.
common_mistakes: Classing the serpent as a woodwind because it is made of wood; it is sounded by buzzing the lips, so acoustically it belongs with the brass or lip-reed family.
Treating the natural rasp as a defect, when the coarse tone is characteristic of these instruments rather than a fault.
Assuming the ophicleide is valved like a modern tuba; it uses keys and tone holes, like a large keyed bugle.
scenario_contexts: Recording a period-instrument ensemble where the serpent doubles the bass line in a church acoustic.
An ophicleide standing in for a tuba in a historically informed performance of early Romantic music.
An engineer choosing mic placement to capture the rasp without harshness.

sources: Baines, Brass Instruments: Their History and Development
Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (serpent; ophicleide)

fields.definition: The sheng's ability to sound several of its free-reed bamboo pipes at once, producing chords or intervals rather than a single line — traditionally parallel fourths and fifths and, on modern instruments, full harmonies — since each reed speaks only when its pipe's finger hole is covered and the player blows or draws air.
fields.plain_english: The sheng is a Chinese mouth organ made of bamboo pipes. Each pipe has a small vibrating metal reed. Unlike a flute or trumpet, it can play several notes at once, so a player can hold a whole chord.
fields.purpose_function: Chord playing lets the sheng provide harmony and sustained accompaniment within an ensemble, a rare trait among wind instruments; the free reeds give steady tone whether the player blows out or draws in.
fields.practical_application: An arranger uses the sheng for held chords and clusters under a melody, and an engineer mics it to capture the blend of several pipes without favoring one reed.
common_mistakes: Thinking the sheng plays only one note at a time like a flute, when it is built to sound several pipes together for chords.
Assuming a pipe sounds when its hole is open; a sheng reed speaks only when the finger hole is covered.
Expecting sound on the out-breath only, when the free reeds sound on both blowing and drawing air.
scenario_contexts: A sheng holding sustained chords beneath a dizi melody in a Chinese orchestra.
A modern keyed sheng playing full harmonies in a contemporary work.
Miking a sheng to blend its stacked pipe tones evenly.

sources: Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (sheng)
Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments (free reeds)

fields.definition: A tone sounded on the shofar — an ancient natural horn made from a ram's or other kosher animal's horn and blown by buzzing the lips like a brass instrument — which, having no finger holes or valves, yields only two or three harmonic pitches; the ritual calls tekiah, shevarim and teruah are its prescribed blasts in Jewish liturgy.
fields.plain_english: A shofar is a ram's horn you play by buzzing your lips, like a simple trumpet with no buttons. Because it has no finger holes, it makes just two or three notes. The loud calls it sounds are its blasts.
fields.purpose_function: The shofar's blast serves as a ceremonial signal and call in Jewish worship, above all at Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur; with no valves or holes it relies on lip tension to reach its few available pitches.
fields.practical_application: An engineer recording a shofar in a service expects a loud, buzzy, narrow-pitch tone and places the mic off the bell axis so the blasts do not overload the input.
common_mistakes: Thinking the shofar can play a melody, when with no holes or valves it sounds only two or three harmonics.
Assuming it is a woodwind; the shofar is lip-blown, so acoustically it is a natural horn in the brass family.
Expecting a smooth, refined tone, when the shofar's voice is meant to be raw and penetrating.
scenario_contexts: Miking a shofar for a Rosh Hashanah service broadcast.
Capturing the tekiah and teruah calls cleanly despite their loud, buzzy peaks.
A sound designer using a shofar blast as a signal or dramatic effect.

sources: Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (shofar)
Baines, Brass Instruments: Their History and Development (animal-horn lip instruments)

fields.definition: A bubbling or crackling sound produced when condensation from the player's warm breath collects in the bore of a wind or brass instrument and disturbs the airflow, typically near valves, tone holes or tubing bends; it is cleared with a water key (spit valve), by emptying slides, or by swabbing.
fields.plain_english: When you blow warm breath into a horn, tiny water drops form inside, like fog on a cold window. When that water pools in the tubing, air bubbling through it makes a gurgle. Players open a little water key to drain it.
fields.purpose_function: The gurgle is a byproduct of condensation, not a musical feature; recognizing it tells the player to drain the instrument so notes speak cleanly instead of sputtering.
fields.practical_application: A brass player empties the water key during a rest to stop gurgling, and a live engineer learns to expect the odd bubbling noise and may edit or ride around it on a recording.
common_mistakes: Thinking the water is mostly saliva, when it is mainly condensation from warm, moist breath cooling inside the metal tubing.
Blaming a gurgle or airy note on the reed or embouchure when the bore simply needs draining.
Forgetting to empty the water key or slides during rests, so notes sputter at the worst moment.
scenario_contexts: A trumpet player draining the water key between phrases to stop a gurgle.
An engineer hearing a bubbling noise on a trombone take and asking for another pass.
A tuba player emptying condensation from the slides during a long rehearsal.

sources: Baines, Brass Instruments: Their History and Development
Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments (condensation in wind instrument bores)

fields.definition: The soft mechanical thump heard on a pipe organ when stops are drawn or retired — the drawknobs, sliders or combination-action pistons moving ranks into or out of play — an incidental noise of the stop action rather than a musical tone.
fields.plain_english: A pipe organ turns sets of pipes on and off using stops. When the player changes stops, the mechanism moves. You can hear a soft thunk, most of all when the preset buttons switch many stops at once.
fields.purpose_function: The thunk is a side effect of the stop or combination action engaging ranks; hearing it confirms the mechanism moved, though a well-regulated action keeps the noise low.
fields.practical_application: An organist times stop changes to musical rests to hide the thunk, and a technician regulates the combination action or slider motors when the noise grows loud or the change is sluggish.
common_mistakes: Mistaking a normal stop-change thunk for a mechanical fault, when a light thump is inherent to slider and combination actions.
Changing many stops during a quiet passage, letting the thunk intrude instead of hiding it in a louder moment or rest.
Ignoring a thunk that grows louder or uneven, which can signal a combination action or slider motor needing service.
scenario_contexts: An organist hitting a general piston mid-piece and hearing the stops thunk in.
A technician regulating an electro-pneumatic combination action to quiet the change.
A recording engineer placing mics to minimize audible stop-change noise during a broadcast.

sources: Audsley, The Art of Organ Building (stop action; combination action)
Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (organ; combination action)

fields.definition: An unwanted squeal or squawk at the moment of strike-in — the start of the bagpipe, when the player fills the bag and strikes it to set the drone and chanter reeds sounding together — caused when the reeds fail to speak cleanly at once under uneven or insufficient bag pressure.
fields.plain_english: A piper starts the pipes by filling the bag and giving it a firm squeeze, so all the reeds sound at once. If the pressure is uneven, a reed can squeak before it settles. That messy start is the strike-in squeal.
fields.purpose_function: A clean strike-in is a mark of good piping; the squeal signals that bag pressure or reed setup is off, so removing it means the drones and chanter speak together crisply.
fields.practical_application: A piper practices a firm, even strike-in to avoid the squeal, and adjusts reed strength or seating when a reed squawks at start-up every time.
common_mistakes: Filling the bag too slowly or with uneven pressure, so a reed squeals instead of the pipes striking in cleanly.
Blaming the squeal on the chanter reed alone when a drone reed or the strike itself is at fault.
Neglecting reed seating and strength, letting the same reed squawk at every start-up.
scenario_contexts: A piper striking in before a competition and fighting a chanter squeal.
A pipe band tuning up where uneven strike-ins cause squeals across the corps.
An engineer recording pipes and editing out a squeal at the start of a take.

sources: Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (bagpipe)
Baines, Bagpipes (Pitt Rivers Museum monograph)
